amalgamate

uh-MAL-guh-mayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To amalgamate is to combine or unite into a single whole.

Chemists watched the two metals amalgamate into a single alloy stronger than either one alone.

Example

After years of friendly rivalry, the two neighboring fire departments chose to amalgamate their equipment and staff into one larger, better-funded department.

Two separate things becoming one combined whole, instead of staying rivals, is exactly what it means to amalgamate.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

merge: When two things merge, they stop being two: the old boundary disappears, and two lanes or two firms go forward as one. To amalgamate stresses the mixing itself -- several separate elements blended into one combined whole, the way two metals amalgamate into a single alloy.

consolidate: To consolidate is to gather scattered pieces into one stronger, tidier whole -- debts consolidated into one loan, offices consolidated onto one floor. Amalgamate points at the blending of the parts themselves; consolidate points at the gain in strength and order the joining achieves.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

separate: keep apart

divide: split into parts

Where it sits · how completely the parts become one — combine → amalgamate → fuse

combine vs. amalgamate: Combine is weaker than amalgamate: combined ingredients may still stay distinct, while amalgamating goes further, blending separate parts into one single whole.

fuse vs. amalgamate: Fuse is stronger than amalgamate: amalgamated companies merge into one organization, but things that fuse join so completely the original pieces can never be told apart.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — amalgam

root — amalgam: a blended mixture, especially an alloy of mercury (Latin/Greek malagma, 'a softening poultice')

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make; to cause to become (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Amalgamate is built from amalgam -- a blended alloy, especially of mercury -- plus -ate, 'to make.' To amalgamate something is to make it into a single blended whole, the way metals combine in an amalgam.

Use the root in a new word: amalgam

Word Choice

Amalgamate is a fairly neutral, almost technical word for combining -- it's equally at home describing companies, chemicals, or committees, without implying anything about generosity or greed.
